elements.content:
• HTML is the foundation of web pages

• Course goals: document structure, basic tags, good practices

• Build a simple personal web page

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Dr. Maya Patel, and today we’re kicking off our journey into web development with an overview of what HTML is all about.
First, HTML—Hypertext Markup Language—is the foundation of every web page. Think of it as the skeleton that gives structure to the content you see in a browser.

Our goals for this lesson are threefold: understand the basic document structure, learn the most common tags like headings, paragraphs, and links, and adopt good practices that keep our code clean and accessible.
By the end of today, each of you will have built a simple personal web page—a single file that introduces yourself to the world. Let’s get started!

<!DOCTYPE html>

    <title>Page Title</title>
  </head>

    Hello, world!
  </body>
</html>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into the building blocks of any web page – the basic HTML document structure.
First, notice the doctype declaration at the very top: <!DOCTYPE html>. This tells the browser that we’re writing an HTML5 document.
Here’s a minimal example. After the doctype, we open an <html> tag, which contains two main sections: the <head> and the <body>.
The html tag acts like the outer shell of the page – everything you write goes inside it.
Inside html, the head section holds meta‑information: the page title, character set, links to stylesheets, and other data the browser needs but you don’t see on the page.
The body is where the visible content lives – headings, paragraphs, images, and so on.
If you look at the simple hierarchy diagram, you can see the nesting: html > head > body. Each layer is contained within the one above it.
To recap, every HTML file starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, then an <html> tag that splits into <head> for metadata and <body> for the page content. That's all you need to get a basic page up and running.

• Create a link: <a href="URL">text</a>

• Insert an image: <img src="path" alt="description">

• Use meaningful alt text for accessibility

• Combine link and image: <a href="URL"><img src="path" alt="description"></a>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into how we add links and images to our web pages.
First, creating a hyperlink is as simple as wrapping the text you want clickable inside an tag, like text.
Next, to embed an image, we use the tag with a source path and an alt attribute: .
Remember, the alt text is crucial for accessibility—it describes the image for people using screen readers.
Finally, you can combine both by placing an tag inside an tag, turning the image itself into a clickable link.
That covers the basics of links and images. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content:
• Ordered list: <ol> with <li>

• Unordered list: <ul> with <li>

• Table tags: <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td>

• Simple schedule table example

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into our topic today: Lists and Tables in HTML.

First, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag and each item is wrapped in <li>. This creates a numbered list. An unordered list works the same way but starts with <ul>, giving you bullet points instead of numbers.
Notice the difference in the opening tags: <ol> versus <ul>. Both rely on <li> for each list entry.

Now let's look at how we build a simple table. We start with <table>, then define rows with <tr>. Inside each row, <th> creates a header cell and <td> creates a regular data cell. This example shows a weekly schedule.
You can see the header row uses <th> for "Day" and "Activity", while the following rows use <td> for the actual schedule entries.
To recap, we covered ordered and unordered lists with <ol>/<ul> and <li>, and we introduced the basic table tags: <table>, <tr>, <th>, and <td>. Great job following along!

elements.content:
• Sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves accessibility and SEO

• Example layout using semantic tags

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into Semantic HTML. This means using tags that describe the meaning of the content, not just how it looks.
First, look at these sectioning elements: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. Each one tells browsers and assistive technologies what role that part of the page plays.
Using them improves accessibility for screen readers and also boosts SEO because search engines understand the structure of your page better.

Here’s a simple layout example. Notice how the <header> sits at the top, the <nav> provides navigation links, the <main> holds the core content broken into <section> and <article> blocks, and the <footer> wraps everything up.
To recap, semantic tags give meaning, help users and search engines, and keep our code organized. Any questions before we move on?

questions.question: Which HTML tag is used for the main heading of a page?
questions.analysis: The <h1> tag defines the most important heading on a page. <header> is a container for introductory content, <title> belongs in the <head> section, and <head> is the document metadata container.

questions.question: Select all HTML elements that are appropriate for creating a navigation bar (choose all that apply).
questions.analysis: <nav> semantically represents a set of navigation links. A list (<ul>) is commonly used inside <nav> to list the links. <section> is for thematic grouping, and <footer> is for page footer content, not navigation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct syntax for displaying an image stored in the file "photo.jpg" with alternative text "A scenic view"?
questions.analysis: The tag uses the src attribute for the image file and the alt attribute for alternative text. The other options use incorrect tag names or attribute names.

actions.text: Alright, let's dive into a quick check on the HTML basics we just covered. Read each question carefully, and remember the key points about headings, navigation structures, and image tags.

For the first question, think about the tag that defines the main heading on a page. It's the one that browsers treat as the most important heading level, and it also helps search engines understand the page's primary topic.

The second question asks you to pick every element that could be part of a navigation bar. Recall that HTML provides a semantic <nav> element specifically for navigation, and that lists (<ul>) are often used inside it to list links. Other containers like <section> or <footer> serve different purposes.

The third question focuses on the correct syntax for displaying an image. Remember that the tag is self‑closing, uses the src attribute for the file path, and the alt attribute for alternative text that describes the image.
